They can be manufactured anywhere, trafficked almost everywhere, and modified overnight to evade control. And challenging public health systems, and the synthetic surge affects all regions. At the same time, global cocaine production and trafficking are breaking record ceilings and meeting rising demand. We also established the ASEAN Narcotics Cooperation Center, under which the ASEAN Drug Monitoring Network was created to facilitate the sharing of information and experience related to illicit drugs monitoring and the development of the ASEAN Drug Monitoring Report. ASEAN recognizes the deep and lasting harm that drugs inflict across our region. Drug abuse continues to destroy many lives, leading many down a path of addiction, poor health, and loss of opportunity. To remember the lives lost to drug abuse, the ASEAN member states will observe the ASEAN Drug Victims Remembrance Day On 26 June, in conjunction with the International Day Against Drug Abuse and Illicit Trafficking. Substances are placed under the various schedules based on scientific assessments of their potential for abuse, dependence, and harm to public health. And we grant priority to structural causes. And community-based responses. At the same time, we have a security policy to deal with transnational organized crime based on reciprocity, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, joint and differentiated responsibility, and mutual confidence. The most recent operation against the most powerful cartel in the country, when its leader ended up dead, is an example of our endeavors to combat this scourge and to involve our partners in this struggle. The division between producing, consumer, and trafficking countries is not just artificial and limited, it is obsolete. Today, the so-called fields in distant rural areas have become laboratories all over the world. The raw materials are now processed chemicals. With design precursors. New drugs are produced closer to consumers. They are transported in smaller volumes. They are more difficult to detect, and they generate more margins. Their name and their color is more important than their origin, and they are increasingly potent, addictive, and lethal. There are praiseworthy efforts underway by many countries to reduce consumption. We hear about them at CND. We are encouraged by actions applied in the world's main market. However, we need to direct our efforts at the abuse or misuse of drugs, especially the overprescription of drugs, not against science, medicine, or health. We would like to make our experience available, as Mexico has traditionally had very low levels of addiction and consumption. Thank you.
Thank you. I have a pleasure to invite His Excellency Mr. Reza Najafi, Ambassador and Permanent Representative of Islamic Republic of Iran. Please, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. Bismillahirrahmanirrahim. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Secretary-General of the Drug Control Headquarters of the Islamic Republic of Iran, who couldn't join us today due to the heinous acts of aggression against the Islamic Republic of Iran. The ongoing atrocities, including killing more than 180 elementary schoolgirls and destruction of 14 hospitals by American and Israeli bombs cannot be justified under any circumstances. Mr. Chairman, let me begin by congratulating Your Excellency on your election as the Chair and assure you of our full support. We also thank the Secretariat for ongoing— for organizing this session. My delegation aligns itself with the statements of the G77 and China, as well as the ASEAN and Pacific Group. We wish to provide the following observations in national capacity. Excellencies, the world drug problem is evolving in increasingly complex and in alarming ways. Despite sustained efforts, we continue to witness rapid proliferation of new psychoactive substances, synthetic drugs, and their precursor chemicals. Also, trafficking networks are employing ever more sophisticated methods, posing challenges to national monitoring and control systems, as as to the international drug control framework. To address this problem, promotion of international cooperation is of paramount importance. Enhancing operational collaborations, reinforcing intelligence-sharing mechanisms, promoting the exchange of best practices, improving early warning systems, expanding technical assistance and provision of equipment and advanced technologies are essential elements of such cooperation. Moreover, balanced preventive and health-oriented strategies must be encouraged. Improving access to controlled substances for scientific and medical purposes while effectively preventing diversion should remain a priority. In this regard, exchange of latest research findings and practical experiences shall be facilitated. In recent years, successful regional mechanisms such as HONELA, Regional Programme for Afghanistan and Neighbouring Countries, and Triangular Initiative have been constrained or only partially operational. Such initiatives need to be supported through predictable, and adequate funding. Impediments in addressing world drug problems, including unilateral coercive measures, have to be swiftly removed. Such unlawful measures increase financial and operational burden associated with implementing drug-related programs and undermine the capacity of frontline states to effectively combat drug trafficking. Mr. Chairman, the Islamic Republic of Iran has adopted a balanced, comprehensive approach to drug control that gives equal weight to supply and demand sides. It also includes special programs for harm reduction and primary prevention. For instance, in 2025, A total of 356 tons of illicit drugs were seized. 1,850 drug trafficking networks were dismantled, and 8,600 addiction treatment and harm reduction centers were operated. My delegation planned to share a successful experience through the side event titled Experience of Iran in Harm Reduction and Hope and the Hope and Life Village Model, which unfortunately was cancelled due to the current unlawful war imposed on my country. In conclusion, I wish to reiterate that addressing the world drug problem is a shared responsibility. Only through genuine multilateralism, solidarity, and sustained commitment can we ensure a more secure, healthy, and resilient future for our society. I thank you, Mr. Chairman.
Thank you. I have the pleasure to invite His Excellency Mr. Dmitry Lyubinsky, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation. Please, you have the floor.

Distinguished Chair, colleagues, Ambassador of Hanyisyan, the ever more complex drug situation jeopardizes international stability, economic development, and human rights. Our country faces a rapid rise in the illicit production of synthetic drugs based on chemical raw materials which were imported from abroad. To counteract this negative trend, in early March Russia reached out to the UN Secretary-General proposing that 4 precursors of methadone and 1 precursor of homemade methadone be placed under international control. We call members of the Commission to support this initiative at the 70th session. The Commission possesses all requisite tools to combat the global drug problem. The international legal regime for drug control has proven its effectiveness, and that regime is turning 65 this year. Any steps involving a deliberate refusal to implement obligations under the 3 conventions or to permit the non-medical use and circulation of drugs in practice end up being harmful for public safety and health and undermine international dialogue. What are also counterproductive are the attempts of a number of countries to impose their own interpretation of certain provisions of the conventions. We call on all to refrain from imposing the tendentious techniques of the so-called harm reduction, which are not applied or which are prohibited at the legislative level in over half of the countries around the world. Cooperation among law enforcement agencies is impeded by a high degree of politicization, which goes as far as deliberately rejecting dialogue. It's important to return to in-person format of Honlio drug control meetings as soon as possible. A successful example of coordination of regional efforts includes such organizations as the CSTO, the SCO, and the CIS, which is the subject of the Russian thematic event to be held today. We welcome honest and open discussion on strengthening the international drug control system, including as part of the interdisciplinary panel of experts experts to be created. The prominent Russian specialist and health professional, Oksana Guseva, has been nominated to that panel. Russia contributes substantially to the global campaign against drug— against drugs through the provision of technical assistance. As part of our voluntary contribution, which has gone up to $3 million jointly with UNODC, we are carrying out projects to train anti-narcotics officers in Central Asia, Iran, Pakistan, Egypt, and also we are carrying out projects in this area of drug prevention, rehabilitation, promoting a healthy lifestyle among the youth. We're grateful to the INCB for their cooperation in enhancing the potential of states of the Global South in implementing the UN Drug Control Conventions and in ensuring the accessibility of narcotic drugs. In 2025, specialized training sessions were provided to African countries. The streamlined actions, integrity, and good faith of countries in implementing their obligations will determine whether lives are saved and whether the public safety and health will be upheld. Russia unwaveringly will continue to take measures to achieve that goal. Thank you.

Thank you. And at this point, I would also I would like to thank the interpreters who agreed to work a little bit more than allotted time to accommodate a couple of more speakers. Chairperson, Acting Executive Director of the UNODC, honorable ministers, distinguished delegates, let me take this opportunity to congratulate you, Chairperson, and your bureau on your election to preside over the 69th Commission on Narcotic Drugs. Zimbabwe would like to assure you of its support and cooperation for the success of this meeting. Zimbabwe aligns itself with the G77 and China and Africa Group statements. Zimbabwe is fully committed to the implementation of the international drug control treaties and to coordinating international cooperation and collaboration towards strengthening all multilateral efforts to overcome the world drug problem. Over the past year, Zimbabwe continued to take a comprehensive multi-sectoral approach aimed at reducing both the supply and demand of illicit drugs, providing treatment and rehabilitation services, and ensuring successful reintegration of drug and substance abuse survivors into society. Zimbabwe intensified its efforts towards combating drug trafficking. This included anti-drug trafficking operations that resulted in the destruction, rather, of illegal drug bases, the confiscation of sizable quantities of illegal drugs and the arrest of over 3,000 suspected drug suppliers each quarter. Collaboration with regional international law enforcement agencies has proven crucial in inception— intercepting cross-border drug traffickers and enhancing enforcement measures. The Medicines Control Authority of Zimbabwe strengthened its compliance inspections that resulted in a reduced availability of illicit drugs and substances within our country. Chairperson, Zimbabwe has intensified demand reduction efforts, particularly targeting young people, working in collaboration with religious and private voluntary organizations. This is being done through educational programs, at every level, from primary school to tertiary institutions, and of course in the communities. Millions of people, including the marginalized, have therefore been reached. Further, the country has continued to harness the power of the media to reach a wider audience. The provision of treatment and rehabilitation services is being strengthened, with a total of 14 rehabilitation centers being fully operational. Furthermore, a whole-of-government and society approach has remained the cornerstone of the country's program. This has resulted in enhanced treatment programs in both the public and the private sector that include incarcerated individuals. The National Committee on Drug and Substance Abuse, alongside with its partners, supported victims in reintegration. Integrating back into communities, offering psychosocial support, and empowering families to assist in the recovery journey of their loved ones. As I conclude, let me reiterate that Zimbabwe remains committed to playing its part, cooperating with the international community in confronting drug and substance abuse while striking a balance between control, availability, and accessibility of controlled drugs for medical and scientific purposes. Our ongoing efforts demonstrate the nation's commitment to addressing the drug problem at every level of the society, leaving no one and no place behind. I thank you.

Thank you very much. And the last speaker of this morning session on our list is distinguished representative of Peru, Mr. Dante Delgado, CEO of National Commission for Development and Life Without Drugs. Please, you have the floor.

Chair, congratulations on your election, and I wish you every success. Distinguished delegates, combating the world drug problem is a priority for Peru. We are the 2nd global producer of cocaine, and my country has been seriously affected by a scourge that has an impact on public safety, the environment, and the most vulnerable populations. For Peru, Dealing with this challenge requires dynamic responses based on the principle of joint and shared responsibility. We are aware that there is no one-stop solution for this problem. We have to consider the different realities, interests, and needs in each context, and therefore we need a solid pillar— the 3 UN drug conventions, and Peru reaffirms its steadfast commitment to them and implements them in a comprehensive way. Our national policy includes decisive supply reduction, public health, and alternative development projects together, also considering gender equality, the empowerment of women, and the protection of vulnerable communities as well as caring for the environment. I would like to acknowledge a very valuable cooperation with strategic allies such as UNODC. Their integrated illicit crop monitoring system has enabled Peru to better understand the dynamics of illegal coca leaf crops and to better target its resources for eradication. Thanks to those efforts, our country has managed to reduce for the second year in a row the surface area of illicit coca crops, going from 92,784 hectares in 2023 to 89,755 in 2024. Moreover, in 2023, We eradicated more than 36,000 hectares, which will be seen in this year's report and which consolidate this downward trend. I'd like to point out that Peru provides reliable data based on UNODC's quality assurance system. Peru's progress has been based on eradication of illicit crops and supply control, and we are countering drugs with alternative development crops. We are following the United Nations guidelines which were adopted in Lima in 2013. Together with Thailand and Germany, we have presented a draft resolution for an additional document to strengthen implementation vis-à-vis new challenges, reducing illicit crops through sustainable economic opportunities. Our experience shows that with political will and a consistent implementation of the 3 conventions in the framework of a comprehensive public policy, it is possible possible to achieve results. I would like to reaffirm that this forum is of huge priority for us in Peru. We believe in commitment building. We believe in comprehensive policies to deal with the world drug problem, and we would like to express our confidence in seeing great steps forward in our joint fight against the world drug problem. Thank you.
